title: About CTM
text:
Why CTM?
Programming and computational thinking have become increasingly important in education, research, and professional life.
However, their integration into university mathematics education remains uneven.
CTM was created to help address this challenge by connecting educational experience across European universities and developing practical resources for teaching and learning.
The ambition is simple: make it easier for students to learn mathematics through computation, and easier for educators to introduce programming into their teaching.

title: About CTM
text:
Our Objectives
CTM was designed around three connected goals.



01. Investigate
Identify challenges, needs, and effective practices for integrating programming into undergraduate mathematics education.




02. Create
Develop accessible tutorials, exercises, and mathematical projects that strengthen computational thinking and programming skills.




03. Connect
Support collaboration and the exchange of educational resources between universities across Europe.

title: About CTM
text:
From Research to Resources
The CTM project was designed to connect educational research with practical teaching materials.

Understanding the Challenges
Surveys and interviews with students and educators were planned to identify needs, obstacles, and existing practices.


Developing Tutorials
The project planned to develop browser-based learning modules to introduce programming and computational thinking in a mathematical context.


Creating Mathematical Projects
The project also aimed to develop exercises and student projects that connect mathematical theory to computational applications.


Supporting Teaching Practice
Another important area was exploring how computational projects can be used, evaluated, and assessed in university teaching.

text:
Mathematics Education in the Age of AI
As generative AI became more widely accessible, new questions emerged about the relationship between programming, mathematical understanding, and teaching.
Although generative AI was not a central part of CTM’s original objectives, its growing influence provides an important perspective on the future of computational mathematics education.

A European Collaboration
CTM brings together five partner universities from across Europe.

Supporting Computational Thinking
Programming can be a powerful tool for exploring mathematical ideas.
However, computational thinking involves more than writing code.
It includes identifying problems, developing algorithms, evaluating solutions, and connecting computational results with mathematical reasoning.
CTM aims to support educators in integrating these approaches into university mathematics teaching.

title: AI & Education
text:
The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence has changed how students and educators interact with programming.
AI tools can now generate code, explain mathematical concepts, and assist with problem-solving.
This creates new opportunities, but also raises important questions about how programming and mathematics should be taught.

title: AI & Education
text:
A New Perspective for CTM
When CTM was originally conceived, the widespread use of generative AI was not a central consideration.
As these technologies became increasingly accessible, questions about their role in mathematics and programming education became more relevant.
This section explores how computational thinking can remain an important educational goal in a changing technological landscape.

title: AI & Education
text:
Questions for Mathematics Education

What Should Students Learn?
If AI can generate working code, which programming skills remain essential for students studying mathematics?
How can computational thinking help students understand, evaluate, and critically use AI-generated solutions?


How Can Educators Adapt?
AI-assisted programming introduces new possibilities for teaching and learning.
It also raises questions about assessment, independent problem-solving, and how students demonstrate understanding.


Using AI Responsibly
AI-generated explanations and code can contain mistakes.
Students therefore need the mathematical knowledge and computational understanding required to evaluate results rather than accepting them uncritically.

Computational thinking is about more than simply writing code.

Breaking down complex problems
Recognizing patterns
Developing algorithms

What is CTM?
Computational Thinking makes sense of Mathematics (CTM) is a European collaborative project focused on integrating programming and computational thinking into university mathematics education.
The project aims to identify teaching needs, develop practical educational resources, and support students and educators across Europe.


01. Understand
Identify challenges, needs, and effective approaches to teaching mathematics with programming.


02. Develop
Create tutorials, exercises, and mathematical projects that support computational thinking.


03. Share
Make educational materials accessible and support their use across European universities.

From Ambition to Impact
CTM was designed to make programming and computational thinking more accessible in university mathematics education.
Its work was organized around several connected areas, from identifying teaching needs to developing educational materials and exploring assessment strategies.
The sections below describe the project’s planned areas of work. Verified results and materials will be added as they are reviewed.



01. Understanding the Needs
Investigating student and educator experiences, existing practices, and obstacles to introducing programming into mathematics teaching.




02. Developing Tutorials
Planning accessible programming tutorials and mathematical learning activities that support computational thinking.




03. Creating Mathematical Projects
Developing approaches to computational exercises and projects that connect mathematical theory with applications.




04. Exploring Assessment
Investigating ways to evaluate students’ computational work and support meaningful learning through programming activities.
